person.name: Alan_Turing
person.summary: Alan Turing was an English mathematician and logician whose work founded theoretical computer science and deeply influenced artificial intelligence, cryptanalysis, and mathematical biology. He formalised the notion of computation with the Turing machine, proved the unsolvability of the Entscheidungsproblem, led key wartime efforts to break German ciphers, designed one of the first stored‑program computers, and later proposed what became known as the Turing test for machine intelligence.

chapters.headline: Colonial Childhood to Sherborne
chapters.description: From birth into a family tied to the British Empire through his intellectually precocious school years at Sherborne, Turing’s early life is shaped by separation from his parents, traditional education, and a rapidly emerging scientific talent.

chapters.headline: Cambridge Foundations of Computation
chapters.description: As an undergraduate and then Fellow at King’s College, followed by doctoral work at Princeton, Turing develops the conceptual framework of computability and oracle machines that will underpin modern computer science.

chapters.headline: Wartime Codebreaking Leadership
chapters.description: With the onset of the Second World War, Turing moves from pure mathematics into cryptanalytic work at Bletchley Park, where he leads Hut 8 in breaking German naval Enigma and plays a central role in Allied signals intelligence.

chapters.headline: Postwar Electronic Computing Vision
chapters.description: After the war, Turing designs the Automatic Computing Engine at the National Physical Laboratory and then joins the Manchester Computing Laboratory, translating his theoretical ideas into some of the earliest practical stored‑program computers while beginning his work on machine intelligence.

chapters.headline: Persecution Morphogenesis Legacy
chapters.description: In his final years at Manchester, Turing formulates the Turing test, endures prosecution and chemical castration for homosexuality, and pioneers mathematical morphogenesis before his untimely death from cyanide poisoning.

events.title: Birth in London
events.description: Alan Mathison Turing is born in London to Julius and Ethel Sara Turing, a British civil servant in India and his Anglo‑Irish wife. The family soon returns to India, while arranging for Alan and his elder brother to be raised and educated in England, giving him early experience of a divided life between empire and home.

events.title: Scientific prodigy at Sherborne
events.description: At 13, Turing enters [[Sherborne School|Sherborne School]], a traditional English public school that prizes the classics over science. Despite some teachers’ doubts about his unconventional interests, he independently works through advanced mathematics and later reads Albert Einstein, apparently rediscovering for himself aspects of Einstein’s critique of Newtonian mechanics. His determination to pursue science, even in an unsympathetic environment, marks him out as an exceptional talent.

Sherborne School.explanation: A long‑established English independent boarding school in Sherborne, Dorset, known in Turing’s time for its strong emphasis on classical studies rather than science or mathematics.

events.title: Death of Christopher Morcom
events.description: Turing’s closest school friend and intellectual companion, Christopher Morcom, dies from complications of bovine tuberculosis. The loss devastates Turing, who responds by throwing himself even more intensely into mathematics and science. In letters to Morcom’s mother he wrestles with questions about mind, matter, and the survival of the spirit, themes that echo through his later scientific and philosophical work.

events.date_note: Date of formal acceptance of his dissertation; fellowship election followed later in 1935
events.title: Elected Fellow of Kings College
events.description: After winning a scholarship and taking first‑class honours in mathematics at King’s College, Cambridge, Turing writes a dissertation on the [[central limit theorem|central limit theorem]] that is accepted in March 1935. On the strength of this work he is elected a Fellow of King’s College that same year, giving him a research post and marking his emergence as a promising young pure mathematician. The fellowship provides the intellectual freedom from which his ideas on computation soon grow.

central limit theorem.explanation: A fundamental result in probability theory stating that the sum (or average) of many independent random variables tends toward a normal (Gaussian) distribution, under broad conditions, regardless of the original variables’ distributions.

events.date_note: Completion and submission date of the paper
events.title: Defines the Turing machine
events.description: Turing completes and submits his landmark paper "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the [[Entscheidungsproblem|Entscheidungsproblem]]." In it he introduces the abstract "[[Turing machine|Turing machine]]" to model computation and proves that no general algorithm can decide all mathematical propositions in a given formal system, answering Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem in the negative. The work, developed independently but alongside Alonzo Church’s results, becomes a foundation of theoretical computer science.

Entscheidungsproblem.explanation: A decision problem in mathematical logic, posed by David Hilbert, asking for a general algorithm to determine whether any given formal statement is provable from axioms.

Turing machine.explanation: An abstract mathematical model of computation consisting of an infinite tape and a read–write head following simple rules, used to formalize the notion of an algorithm.

events.date_note: Year he received the PhD at Princeton
events.title: Doctorate at Princeton
events.description: Turing spends two years at Princeton University under Alonzo Church, where he completes his PhD thesis, later published as [[Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals|Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals]]. The dissertation explores how to strengthen formal systems by iterating consistency‑strengthening steps along the ordinal numbers and introduces the notion of [[oracle computation|oracle computation]]. This work deepens his logical foundations and forges an important link between American and British research in the nascent theory of computation.

Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals.explanation: Alan Turing's 1938 Princeton PhD dissertation, in which he developed "ordinal logics" to analyze and extend formal mathematical systems beyond the limits shown by Gödel's incompleteness theorems.

oracle computation.explanation: A theoretical model of computation in which a Turing machine is allowed to query an abstract "black box" (an oracle) that can instantly solve a specified decision problem, used to study relative computability and degrees of unsolvability.

events.date_note: Shortly after the outbreak of the Second World War he joined the Government Code and Cypher School
events.title: Joins Bletchley Park codebreakers
events.description: On the outbreak of the Second World War, Turing joins the [[Government Code and Cypher School|Government Code and Cypher School]], working at Britain’s wartime codebreaking centre, later famous as [[Bletchley Park|Bletchley Park]]. Drawing on his theoretical work and his talent for practical ingenuity, he begins attacking German Enigma ciphers, quickly becoming central to the effort to read enemy communications. His move from pure logic into classified wartime service transforms both his own career and the course of the conflict.

Government Code and Cypher School.explanation: The British government’s pre‑GCHQ codebreaking and signals intelligence organisation, responsible for intercepting and deciphering foreign communications before and during the Second World War.

Bletchley Park.explanation: A country estate in Buckinghamshire used as the main British codebreaking centre during the Second World War, where teams worked to decrypt Axis communications such as Enigma.

events.date_note: Represents his main period leading Hut 8 and developing bombe techniques against naval Enigma
events.title: Leads Hut 8 and breaks naval Enigma
events.description: Turing takes charge of [[Hut 8|Hut 8]], the section responsible for German naval cryptanalysis, and designs key methods and electromechanical devices to accelerate breaking Enigma keys, refining and extending prewar [[Polish techniques|prewar Polish techniques]]. His work on the [[bombe|bombe]] and on specialised procedures for U‑boat traffic enables the Allies to read large volumes of German messages, contributing decisively to the Battle of the Atlantic and the protection of convoys. Throughout this period he works with figures such as Gordon Welchman and Joan Clarke in a highly secret, intensely collaborative environment.

Hut 8.explanation: A section of the British codebreaking centre at Bletchley Park dedicated primarily to breaking German naval Enigma ciphers during the Second World War.

Polish techniques.explanation: Refers to cryptanalytic methods developed before the war by Polish mathematicians of the Cipher Bureau, notably Marian Rejewski and colleagues, to attack the Enigma machine.

bombe.explanation: An electromechanical device, originally devised by Polish cryptologists and significantly redesigned in Britain, used to speed up the process of finding Enigma encryption keys.

events.date_note: Covers his postwar tenure at the National Physical Laboratory working on the ACE design
events.title: Designs Automatic Computing Engine
events.description: After the war, Turing joins the National Physical Laboratory and sets out a detailed design for the [[Automatic Computing Engine|Automatic Computing Engine (ACE)]], one of the earliest proposals for a high‑speed stored‑program electronic computer. His ACE reports specify a powerful architecture and programming concepts that anticipate later computer designs, though institutional delays hinder full realisation of the machine under his direction. The work shows him translating his abstract theory of computation into a practical blueprint for electronic computing.

Automatic Computing Engine.explanation: A pioneering electronic, stored-program computer project proposed by Alan Turing at the UK National Physical Laboratory in the mid‑1940s, intended to be one of the fastest and most advanced general‑purpose computers of its time.

events.title: Joins Manchester Computing Laboratory
events.description: Turing accepts Max Newman's invitation to join the [[Computing Machine Laboratory|Computing Machine Laboratory]] at the University of Manchester, which is developing some of the first operational [[stored-program computers|stored‑program computers]]. There he contributes to the design and programming of the Manchester computers and turns his attention to practical issues of numerical computation, as well as beginning his celebrated work on machine intelligence. The Manchester period cements his role as both a visionary theorist and a working computer scientist.

images.caption: The University of Manchester commemorates Alan Mathison Turing (1912-1954) A creator of Computer Science, Code Breaker and Mathematician. Reader in Mathematics, 1948-1954

Computing Machine Laboratory.explanation: Also known as the Royal Society Computing Machine Laboratory, this was the research group at the University of Manchester, led by Max Newman, that built the Manchester Baby and subsequent early electronic computers.

stored-program computers.explanation: Early electronic computers that store both program instructions and data in the same read–write memory, an architecture that became standard for modern computers.

events.date_note: Published in the journal Mind in late 1950
events.title: Introduces the Turing test
events.description: Turing publishes "[[Computing Machinery and Intelligence|Computing Machinery and Intelligence]]" in the philosophy journal Mind, proposing his famous "Imitation Game" as a way to discuss whether machines can think. The paper defines what is now called the Turing test and addresses a range of philosophical objections to machine intelligence, shifting the question from inner consciousness to observable behaviour in conversation. It becomes a foundational text in the philosophy and early history of artificial intelligence.

Computing Machinery and Intelligence.explanation: A 1950 paper by Alan Turing, published in the journal Mind, that introduces the idea now known as the Turing test for machine intelligence and systematically answers philosophical objections to artificial intelligence.

events.date_note: Month approximated; his arrest and trial occurred in early 1952
events.title: Prosecution and chemical castration
events.description: In early 1952 Turing is prosecuted under British law for homosexual acts after reporting a burglary and thereby revealing his relationship with another man. Convicted, he accepts a course of hormone injections—commonly described as chemical castration—as an alternative to imprisonment. The conviction strips him of security clearance and brings intense personal and professional hardship, casting a long shadow over his final years.

events.date_note: Year from publication; month approximate for the appearance of the paper in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
events.title: Publishes morphogenesis theory
events.description: Turing publishes "[[reaction–diffusion theory|The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis]]", applying reaction–diffusion equations to explain how patterns such as spots, stripes, and spirals can develop in living organisms from initially uniform conditions. The paper inaugurates what are now called Turing patterns and becomes a classic in theoretical biology, far ahead of experimental confirmation of such mechanisms. It shows his ability late in life to open an entirely new research field beyond logic and computing.

reaction\u2013diffusion theory.explanation: A mathematical framework in which interacting chemical substances both react with each other and diffuse through space, showing how stable spatial patterns can spontaneously emerge from an initially uniform mixture.

events.title: Death from cyanide poisoning
events.description: Turing dies at his home in [[Wilmslow|Wilmslow]] from cyanide poisoning at the age of 41. A coroner’s inquest rules the death a suicide, though some later commentators note that an accident cannot be entirely ruled out. His passing cuts short an extraordinary career that had already reshaped logic, computing, wartime intelligence, and mathematical biology.

Wilmslow.explanation: A town in Cheshire, England, where Turing had a house on Hollymeade and where he was living at the time of his death in 1954.
